title: The Acquisition Program
text:
The morning report was one line, in one hand.

06:00 — B. ON LEAVE. SHIFTS COVERED. NOBODY TOUCHES HER MIRROR.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it standing in his doorway in yesterday's clothes. On the windowsill, two spent casings had been joined overnight by four more — the whole night's spend, set out in a row. A freshly loaded <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> sat on the counter beside them and said nothing about it. Across the hall, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s door stayed closed. She'd been at her bench since 03:00; he'd heard the music come on, very low, around four. He didn't knock. The wall between them was the help she wanted this morning, and he left it standing.

He put on his coat. He put on <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>. The bike's plate cover sat folded on the table where a terminal used to live, and he left it there, and took the stairs, and walked.

The walk to the Loop took fifty-one minutes. He wanted the distance measured in something that cost him.

It cost him more than distance. Three blocks from the door a man fell in behind him — matched pace, kept it, made no attempt to close. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't check his mirrors. That was the first rule of someone following you: you looked, and they knew you knew, and the whole thing collapsed into something faster and messier than either of you wanted at that hour. Better to let them think they were still invisible. He changed streets twice to be sure and the man changed with him, unhurried, the gap between them exact and never closing. Whoever had ordered B. onto leave had put eyes on the one who'd argued against it, and the eyes wanted him to know.

At the mouth of an alley <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> slowed, gave the man his chance, and none came — the follower simply stopped at the corner and waited, content to watch him keep walking, content that watching was enough. He couldn't lose the tail without turning the walk into the fight he'd left the plate cover home to avoid, and he couldn't reach the Loop without leading it there. The distance stopped being a thing he spent and became a thing spent on him, each of the fifty-one minutes a minute someone else was buying, and there was no street left that didn't run through them.

He knew something was wrong from the top of the underlevel stairs. The dumpling franchise next to the watch-repair had its shutter down at 09:00 on a working Tuesday, and the only thing that closed a dumpling shop on a Tuesday was the block deciding to be elsewhere for an hour.

The stationery shop's bell was lying on the floor.

Someone had taken it off its curl of spring steel and set it down — not broken, removed, the way professionals remove a thing that announces customers. The door stood open. From the corridor drifted a chemical bite that burned the back of the throat, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s implant parsed it before he could: industrial-grade document processor. The kind that ate paper and left nothing behind but ash and a signature in the air. Inside, among the hundred years of drawers, the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> was doing inventory.

Three of them. Gray coveralls over soft armor, archive cases on dollies, white gloves — actual white gloves, the kind evidence handlers wear. Two were loading cardboard boxes marked in <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s own handwriting, his filing system, his whole pre-digital inventory stacked and ready to move. A fourth stood at the counter in a gray suit cut from the same bolt as <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Mr. Able</entity>'s, reading a manifest off his overlay in the bored cadence of a man who did this often.

"—seventeen line items, full provenance, originals and duplicates," the suit was saying. "Triple book value, paid on signature. The Office is closing its local accounts, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>. It prefers the paper closed with them."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity> stood behind his counter with his glasses on and his hands folded. From the doorway <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could see that his hands were perfectly steady. The pot sat cold on its worn ring, no cups out, the surface of what remained in it gone to a skin.

No tea. In three visits across a season — through stolen bikes and customer lists and a war's worth of business — there had always, always been tea.

The suit turned a page in the air. "The juvenile file," he said, checking it against something only he could see. "All documentation related to minors, sealed records, subscription archives. That's part of the transaction."

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s jaw tightened by a fraction that cost him something.

"Every record in this shop is a person's second chance, <entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">Mr. Able</entity>'s colleague," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said, and his voice was quiet, which made it worse. "You came in with a number and a dolly and you started loading. I let you load. I didn't say yes."

"The value is generous," the suit said. "Triple, on signature. You understand what your discretion is worth to us."

"I understand what you're buying with it." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> didn't raise his voice, didn't move his folded hands. "You want to buy my silence, my complicity in whatever you're erasing. That doesn't have a book value. That doesn't price."

"We can return with a seizure order."

"You can. And I'll file with the reciprocity network before your dolly clears the arcade — every dealer from here to Milwaukee will know <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> strong-arms independent vendors, and they'll adjust your terms on every acquisition after this one. That's bad for your budget. That's bad for the board." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> let it sit. "So you can come back with paper. Or you can put my life back on my shelves and leave."

The suit's expression did not change. He was a man who had already filed the next step and was only waiting for the paperwork to catch up. He looked at the two in coveralls. One was already turning toward the boxes, running the reverse logistics in his head.

"Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said, without turning his head. "You find me in a meeting."

The suit turned. The two coverall men by the drawers straightened with the smooth economy of people whose job had a clause in it for this, and the third, nearest the door, shifted to put <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> in his lane.

The suit looked <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> over — saya, coat, the face from a file he had certainly read — and made the professional choice to stay pleasant.

"This is a commercial transaction," he said, not looking up from the manifest. "It doesn't concern walk-ins."

"He's not a walk-in," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "He's a subscriber." He unfolded his hands and laid them flat on the counter and addressed the suit the way he addressed everything, in terms. "Let me restate your offer so the record is clean. The Office wishes to buy, at triple, every document in this shop that touches its local operation. Its shells, its desks, its clearing arrangements, its consultant engagements, its purchases. Including," and his voice did not change at all, which was how <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew, "item seventeen. The juvenile file."

"The Office's paper is <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity>'s business," the suit said. "Clean closure. No audit, no complications. You retire with a number that lets you retire."

"No," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>.

The word sat in the shop like a dropped drawer. The suit blinked. Somewhere in his overlay was a number for this, and it was not a large number, because in forty years this had never happened. Near the archive cases one of the coverall men paused mid-drawer, a folder half-extended, waiting for the next instruction that had not come.

"You're declining triple?"

"I am declining the sale." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took off his half-glasses, folded them, and set them on the counter — a man clearing his hands. "Your office bought a file about a child, for leverage, through a desk you dressed up because you knew I would not sell it to you straight. You made me a party to it. The product of this shop is accuracy, and you used my accuracy to put a wand against a fourteen-year-old's collar." He looked at the suit with no heat at all, which was somehow the coldest thing in the room. "The paper stays. The paper is the only honest witness this trade has. Buying the witness is what guilty institutions do, and this counter does not service that. Not at triple. Not at any multiple. Good morning."

The suit said the odds out loud, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> respected. "There are three of us, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, and the dollies are already loaded."

"And the manifest of what's on them is already in four other shops," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said pleasantly. "I have twenty-three reciprocity arrangements and I used six of them at dawn. Roll those dollies out that door unsigned and every desk in the trade reads the theft by lunch — itemized, with your faces. The Office can buy a great many things. It cannot buy back being known." He put his glasses back on. "Also, the gentleman behind you has been to the destination on your manifest, and your office wrote a no-damage clause about him once. It's very specific about what happens if you leave this location in any state other than the one you found it. I'd review it."

Three sets of eyes made the trip — saya, hands, face, file — and arrived where that trip always arrived.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. Moving would have been a second argument, and the room only needed one. He stood in the doorway with the morning behind him and let them read the night on him: six casings' worth of it, a yard's worth, twelve tons' worth.

The suit closed his overlay.

"The Office will note your position," he told <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, in the tone of a man already drafting the memo that explained this away. "Stand down," he added, quieter, to the coverall men. "Replace everything. Exactly as you found it."

The white gloves unloaded the dollies — every folder back in its drawer, supervised by <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s pointing finger, that one goes under C, no, lower, thank you — the cases lifted off the dollies and stacked, the manifest torn in half and set both pieces on the counter. It took fourteen minutes. Then they filed out past <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> one at a time, quiet, men who had priced the fight and folded. The last one stooped, without being asked, and put the bell back on its spring.

It rang when the door shut behind them. The shop exhaled.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let out a breath he had been holding since the doorway. He looked at his hands — steady, which surprised him — and then at the boy's file still sitting in its drawer, still closed, still only a file and not yet a weapon. He did not know what <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> intended to do with it. He did not know what he intended to do with <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>. He knew only that the file existed, that <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> wanted it badly enough to send three men and an overlay full of numbers, and that whatever came next would require him to have a position on the matter before <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> found a fourth approach that <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s twenty-three arrangements could not cover.

"Now," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>, and lit the burner under the pot — the good one, the cracked glaze that meant something — "tea."

He poured two cups and set <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s down with the handle aimed outward. For a while the only sound was the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> coming up through the tiles and the pot ticking as it cooled. When <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> finally spoke, he did it the way he did everything: by stating the terms.

"Files involving children are sold at children's rate, to children, for the purposes of children. That is the term. It is the one term I have never negotiated. Eleven days ago the <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> bought item seventeen through a cutout I failed to inspect, because they paid early, and paid exactly, and the presentation was perfect." He turned his cup a quarter-turn on its saucer. "I sold a defective product, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. First one in forty years. You watched what it cost me to say no to the recall."

"You said no to triple."

"I said no to laundering my own ledger." He drew a single page from beneath the counter — good stock, the ink dark and exact, folded the particular way — and set it between them. "Customer loyalty disclosure. One fact, free, no record of transmission."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> unfolded it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019ee6a2-c508-774b-a5ff-f923f2c26aab">MR. ABLE</entity>. <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> — LOCAL PRINCIPAL.
TEA HOUSE: <entity repo="character" guid="019e9e4f-1beb-71dd-9071-1877cab7d04d">MERIDIAN</entity> PAVILION, THIRD UNDERLEVEL, LAKEVIEW ADJACENT. STANDING RESERVATION: TUESDAYS AND FRIDAYS, 10:00–12:00.
SECURITY: TWO ADVANCE, TWO INSIDE, ONE EXTERIOR, ONE MOBILE. ROTATION: FORTY MINUTES.
HABIT: CORNER TABLE, NORTHEAST. BACK TO WALL.

"I sell maps, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> said. "Here is a map. What you do at the destination is the destination's business."

It was the same sentence as the first visit, word for word. Both of them sat a moment with the distance between the two deliveries. The first time it had been a philosophy. This time it was one girl on leave and a one-line log.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put the page in his coat. He drank the tea. It was very good, and he said so, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> took the compliment with the small nod of a man whose product had never been the problem.

"One more thing, since you're a subscriber." <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s voice went back to commerce, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> understood as the man returning himself to the shelf. "Your file is now the most requested item in this shop. Four standing orders for updates. I will keep selling it — that's the term you walked in under, and terms don't bend for liking a customer." A beat. "But updates are filed at my discretion as to timing, and I am a very busy man this quarter. Some drawers may not get refiled until... oh. Spring."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him. The cleanest hands in the city poured a second cup, steady as a level.

"That's the closest thing to a kindness you've ever said out loud."

"It's inventory management," said <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>. "Get out of my shop. Destinations keep business hours."

The logbook channel chirped when he got home, his coat still on — a new entry growing under the morning's one line, in a different hand, pressed hard:

14:20 — B. CAME UP TO THE ROOF. SAT WATCH ONE HOUR. DIDN'T LOG ANYTHING. WE DIDN'T EITHER.
14:21 — CORRECTION: LOGGING IT. THIS LOG IS HONEST. SHE CAME BACK. THAT GOES IN THE LOG.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> on the counter next to its six casings and filled the kettle and stood at the window while it came up, looking east toward the Loop. A shop with a brass bell was open for business there, between a watch-repair and a dumpling franchise. This morning, for the price of one term kept, the most temperatureless man in the city had picked a side and called it inventory management.

The kettle clicked.

Three days on, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Casper Vey</entity>'s shop was still three blocks from the target building. Sable said that was either the most useful fact of the morning or the most alarming one. She'd asked which. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had said: "If the building burns, I'd like the story."

The crew ate at the <entity repo="faction" guid="019d6143-a893-7801-860b-0eda6a216393">Lotus</entity> counter on the second floor of the place across the street — the one with no sign and the best view — because <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had spent his marker there at 09:00 and the branch had put up exactly as many chairs as they needed. Nothing was said about it. Nobody at the truce counter touched a weapon, by custom, by the terms the lacquered marker bought. So the crew ate ramen in view of the gray office tower they meant to take apart, and the Narrows ran its ordinary morning underneath them.

One line came from the end of the counter, where a woman with a red braid and aperture-ring eyes was eating with professional focus. Chromatophore panels down her left leg cycled through a freight company's livery at half-brightness — the legal minimum, which meant she had opinions about her sponsor. "Marker spends once. It's spent."

"I know what I bought," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"You bought passage. The door, the hall, six floors of occupied building." Sable put her spoon down. "You did not buy an extraction if this goes sideways."

"I bought us a table. Professionals eat before they work."

Down the counter, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> spooned broth without taking her eyes off the loading dock across the street, guessing weights from the shape of the freight entry. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> ate fast, both hands, already somewhere else in her head. Marisol held her bowl in both hands and looked at nothing, which was how she looked at everything. Freelance verification, a three-year trade acquaintance — a Read who charged what the market thought she was worth, then another thirty percent for the part the market kept pretending wasn't real.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> set his chopsticks across the empty bowl and made the ask he'd come to make. "So confirm my window. Marker holds the door open six floors deep. That's the plan. Tell me it holds?"

The woman with the red braid didn't look up from her bowl. She wiped her mouth once, unhurried, and only then let the aperture-rings widen enough to catch the light. "Marker holds the door," she said. "It doesn't hold Casper's temper." She pulled a folded receipt from her jacket — the kind of paper that moved between shops, customer disclosure, the trail <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> always said never lied — and slid it down the lacquer so <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could read the line. *Marker restriction filed per client request. No transaction. No fee.* Dated that morning, 09:40, forty minutes after his marker went up. "He spent his last favor with the branch to have it quietly downgraded — courtesy passage only, no floors. You've got the lobby and the stairwell. Everything above the second landing, you're trespassing on your own money."

"He sold the downgrade."

"No." She folded the receipt back into her jacket. "He filed it himself. Didn't delegate. Wanted his own hand on the pen." She tipped her chin at the gray tower. "And he knows you're eating here. He picked the counter you'd choose. That's not a man covering his back. That's a man drawing a line in daylight and making sure you see where it is."

Nobody's spoon moved. The table <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had bought to look like patience now looked like exactly what it was — six people sitting still in a window, three blocks from a man who'd already moved. Under the floor the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> came up through the tiles, steady, indifferent, the second heartbeat that lived in the bones of every building in the Narrows.

The logbook entry, filed at 11:47, read: CREW ATE BEFORE. (SABLE HAD THE SPICY ONE. THIS LOG IS FACTUAL.)

At 12:00 the first thing arrived.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had promised it by freight delivery. "I need a counterweight situation," she'd told the rigger's cooperative, "arriving at the loading dock at noon with a valid manifest, because I am going in with the counterweight." The cooperative asked no further questions, because <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> had a credit history and <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity>'s credit history had opinions. What arrived was a machinery crate — five tons on a crane arm, a load that legitimately needed the freight lift and a <entity repo="contract" guid="5d9e2a7c-4f1b-6308-7e5a-2d9c1f4b7308">second opinion</entity> at the dock. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> was inside it, with her tools and the patience of a rigger who had been in tighter spots.

The loading dock's freight manager studied the manifest. It was immaculate. He processed it.

At 12:14 the freight lift signed for five tons and a good-morning nod. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-6eb0-7176-9136-790a0ed124fb">Gantry</entity> stepped off on the third sub-floor and started disabling things, methodically.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> came in through a wall.

Not a door - a wall, because she had read the blueprints and the blueprints said STRUCTURAL, which to <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> meant "challenge" and nothing else. The south face was ferrocrete and carbon composite, state-of-the-art when the tower went up in the 2080s and state-of-the-art still, through sheer inertia and the fact that nobody had ever bothered to upgrade it. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> looked at it the way a locksmith looks at a door.

The thermal lance was built in a shop below a storage unit in the <entity repo="corponation" guid="019d6143-a7a5-7dfd-8f9f-91502211ef14">Ashgrave</entity> fringe - <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity>'s shop, <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity>'s tools, a two-handed industrial piece she'd bench-tuned herself. She set the stand. Locked the angle. Stepped back.

She fired it up at 12:22. The lance was subsonic - nobody at street level heard it, just a sustained hiss like something large was venting. The beam was invisible until it touched something, and what it touched stopped being solid. The ferrocrete didn't so much burn as disappear, turning to ash and vapor in a line seven centimeters wide, the edges glowing orange as the heat bled away from the cut. The air around it went white and shimmered. <entity repo="character" guid="019eb6eb-8f41-7b5d-8c7e-fc6b4e74dc25">Furnace</entity> held the angle steady, letting the laser do what fire does better than any human hand could manage, watching the wall surrender in real time. The secret was patience and the certainty that whatever was on the other side wanted to let you in about as much as the wall did.

She killed the lance. The cut was waist-high, horizontal, long enough for a body to fit through if the body moved fast. She checked the seal on her gloves - the burn scars on her hands were old enough that new ones wouldn't change her grip - and pulled herself through in one motion, shoulders first, the rest following, the ferrocrete still hot enough to blister radiating against her clothes.

"That's me IN," she said, to no one, and stepped through.
